name: Thai Song
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. [...] It is noteworthy that of the four languages here studied, Siamese has by far the greatest number of such weak syllables, Red Tai somewhat fewer, Black Tai still fewer, and in White Tai they are infrequent.
new_statements.citation: Gedney, William J. 1989 [1964]. A comparative sketch of White, Black and Red Tai. In R. J. Bickner, J. Hartmann, T. J. Hudak & P. Peyasantiwong (eds.), Selected Papers on Comparative Tai Studies (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 29), pp. 415-461. Ann Arbor: Center for South and Southeast Asian Studies, University of Michigan. [Originally Social Science Review, special number 14 (1964): 1-47.]
new_statements.locator: p. 421 (section TONES, end of the Red Tai tone list, just before 'Comparison of tones'); PDF page 7; scanned in lines 328-341, verified against the page image
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: The passage is on p. 421 of Gedney 1989 [1964] exactly as quoted (checked against the rendered page image of PDF p. 7 of; scanned lines 328-341 of; the elided middle sentence is Gedney's note that the phenomenon is 'so infrequent in the type of words that we are dealing with' that he marks it with a breve, e.g. S maphraaw4 'coconut'). The p. 418 remark that transcriptions are of syllables 'as pronounced in isolation' is also there. IDENTITY: Not OK for thai1259. Gedney (pp. 415-418) states his Black Tai data come from a family from Muang Piang (44 km NW of Son La) met at Tung Nghia, South Vietnam, and from Bac Cam So of Ban Chieng Di (35 km NW of Son La) in Vientiane, i.e. Tai Dam of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Black Tai words consist of full ('normal') tone-bearing syllables; the only unstressed syllables are reduced presyllables (short a, tone neutralised to mid) that precede a full syllable, so in a sesqui-/disyllabic word of this type prominence is on the final, full syllable. Black Tai has few such weak presyllables (fewer than Siamese or Red Tai). No rule is given for compounds of two full syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak syllables 'sometimes' have vowels other than short a; phenomenon said to be infrequent in Black Tai and to need fuller analysis per language.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; transcriptions are of syllables 'as pronounced in isolation' (p. 418), i.e. citation forms; Gedney notes connected speech has further modifications. Variety described is Black Tai (Tai Dam) of Son La speakers recorded among refugees in South Vietnam/Vientiane, i.e. the parent variety of Thai Song, not Thai Song as spoken in Thailand.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Gedney 1964/1989 p. 421) describes Black Tai = Tai Dam as spoken by Son La (NW Vietnam) speakers, Glottolog taid1247 (ISO blt), the parent variety from which the Thai Song (thai1259, ISO soa) communities of Phetchaburi etc. descend (migrated c. 200 years ago from Muang Thaeng). Burusphat 2012 treats 'Thai Song or Tai Dam (Black Tai)' as one language (codes soa, blt). Every Thai Song-specific description that could be opened (Burusphat 2011, 2012, 2013; Yensamut 1981 [Samut Sakhon]; Jirananthanaporn 2007 [Phitsanulok]) is silent on stress, so the catalog entry, if made, should be flagged as resting on a Tai Dam (Vietnam) proxy pending Maneewong 1987 or Burusphat 2013.

sources.note: p. 421: besides normal (full) syllables, Black Tai (with White Tai, Red Tai, Siamese) has weak-stressed syllables 'usually prefixed to a normal syllable', with short a and tone neutralised to mid; Black Tai has few such syllables. Transcription is of syllables 'as pronounced in isolation' (p. 418). Variety: Black Tai of Son La refugees (Tai Dam proper), not Thai Song of Thailand.
